research: https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/ai-machine-learning/ultimate-prompting-guide-for-nano-banana — Google's own guide: write it as a brief (subject, setting, camera, light, style), not a list of keywords
https://runware.ai/docs/models/google-nano-banana-2/guides/prompting — name the camera angle and depth of field; models treat text as texture, so keep any written words short and few
https://fliki.ai/blog/nano-banana-2-prompting-guide — NB2 reads a prompt as instructions to satisfy, so state counts and positions plainly (e.g. 'exactly four bags')

https://www.cardfactory.co.uk/blog/party-inspiration/the-best-kids-party-bag-ideas/ — UK party bags are handed out at the END of the party as each guest leaves; small paper bags with handles, stickers, bubbles, a slice of cake in a napkin
https://www.mumsnet.com/articles/kids-party-bag-ideas — the UK ritual: one bag per child, name on it, collected at the door on the way out
notes: Honesty to the numbers: the reveal shows exactly FOUR untouched named party bags left on the table for the ONE child leaving with nothing, which is the 4-to-1 ratio counting second homes (571,079 homes that are nobody's main home vs 134,210 homeless households); the narrator's 'already had one' maps the extra bags to second homes and empties. The setup establishes the hall and the crowded table (the plenty); the reveal is the end of the night. No numbers written in either image, so nothing can misread. The child is only ever a small figure from behind in a coat (refusal risk with children), no faces; names on the bags are invented first names, no brands. Look follows Jack's reference: night, cheap colour film, grain, cold fluorescent teal, slightly eerie; the party colours (balloons, bunting) are kept but drained under the tubes, which helps the 'party's over' feeling. The bags carry no handwritten text in the reveal beyond a name each, so the model has little lettering to garble.
